mainTopic: Whether a buyer's vessels (כליו של לוקח) can acquire items for him in places he does not own: the public domain, an alleyway, a shared courtyard, and the seller's own property.
overview: The גמרא first defends רב פפא against a ברייתא that seems to say a buyer's vessels acquire for him even in the real רשות הרבים. It answers that the ברייתא means a סמטא (alleyway). It also explains that 'a courtyard that belongs to neither of them' means a courtyard owned by both partners together. Then רב ששת asks רב הונא whether a buyer's vessels acquire for him when they sit in the seller's property. רב הונא proves they do from the משנה in גיטין about a גט thrown into a woman's lap or basket. רב נחמן rejects this proof, because many אמוראים, and רבי יוחנן as explained by רבא, limit that משנה to special cases. Next the גמרא tries to prove the opposite from a ברייתא about acquiring in the seller's domain. That ברייתא turns out to be about whose vessels the goods are in, so it does not settle the question. Finally רבא brings a new ברייתא about a buyer who pulled donkey drivers and laborers carrying goods into his house, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Does the ברייתא mean the actual public domain?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the ברייתא is talking about the real רשות הרבים, which would contradict רב פפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What, isn't the ברייתא talking about the actual public domain?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא. It suggests that the ברייתא it just quoted says a buyer's vessels acquire for him even in the real public domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב פפא, a buyer's vessels do not acquire for him in the real רשות הרבים. If the ברייתא means the true public domain, it says the opposite. The question 'מאי לאו' pushes the reader toward the reading that causes the problem.

keyTerms.meaning: What, isn't it…? A way of suggesting a reading that creates a difficulty
The public domain, an area open to everyone

phrases.english: What, is it not
phrases.notes: This is about the ברייתא quoted just before this line, which mentions the public domain.

phrases.english: in the actual public domain?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of רב פפא's ruling from earlier on the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's view that a buyer's vessels do not acquire in the real public domain
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read plainly, the ברייתא says the vessels do acquire in רשות הרבים.

steps.title: No, the ברייתא means an alleyway
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a סמטא, not the real public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב פפא by saying the ברייתא's 'public domain' is really a סמטא, a side alleyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סמטא is a quieter area where people have some shared rights, so it is not truly crowded public space. A buyer's vessels can acquire there, and that fits רב פפא.

keyTerms.meaning: An alleyway or side street, a semi-public area

phrases.english: No; an alleyway.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means the real רשות הרבים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means a סמטא, so it does not contradict רב פפא.

steps.title: But it is compared to a courtyard owned by neither
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא puts this place alongside a courtyard that belongs to neither party, so it should mean a place where neither has rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא teaches it alongside a courtyard that does not belong to either of them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the alleyway answer. The ברייתא compares this place to 'a courtyard that belongs to neither of them.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A courtyard owned by neither side sounds like a place where neither the buyer nor the seller has any rights. Both of them do have some rights in a סמטא. So the comparison suggests the ברייתא means the real public domain after all.

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard that does not belong to either of them

phrases.english: But it is similar to a courtyard
that is not of both of them, that it teaches!
phrases.notes: Literally 'not of the two of them.' It sounds like a place where neither of them has any rights.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא דּוּמְיָא דְּחָצֵר שֶׁאֵינָהּ שֶׁל שְׁנֵיהֶם קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא means a סמטא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's comparison points to a place where neither party has rights, and that does not describe an alleyway.

steps.title: The courtyard is owned by both together
steps.stepSummary: 'A courtyard not of both of them' means a jointly owned courtyard that does not belong entirely to either one.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'a courtyard that is not of both of them' mean? It also means one that does not belong entirely to this one or entirely to that one, but to both of them together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rereads the courtyard phrase. It means a courtyard that the two own as partners, not one that neither owns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under this reading, both places in the ברייתא are shared spaces. The partners' courtyard and the סמטא are a good match. רב פפא's view stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is talking about shared spaces, a סמטא and a partners' courtyard. That is why it does not contradict רב פפא.

phrases.english: What is 'a courtyard that is not of both of them' also?
That it is not entirely this one's
and not entirely that one's;
rather, it is of both of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי חָצֵר שֶׁאֵינָהּ שֶׁל שְׁנֵיהֶם נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3 and closes the defense of רב פפא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Not of both of them' means neither party owns it.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means a courtyard owned jointly, which matches the סמטא.

steps.title: Buyer's vessels in the seller's property
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת asks רב הונא whether a buyer acquires items placed in his own vessels while the vessels sit in the seller's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת asked רב הונא: if the buyer's vessels are in the seller's property, does the buyer acquire, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question opens. If the merchandise is put into the buyer's container but the container is on the seller's property, does the buyer own it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person's vessels usually acquire for him. Here, though, they sit in the seller's space, and the seller's property might 'hold' the items for the seller. The question is which one wins.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת מֵרַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet asked of Rav Huna:
The vessel of the buyer in the domain of the seller:
does the buyer acquire, or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת מֵרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new question about where a buyer's vessels can acquire.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a buyer's vessels acquire for him when they are in the seller's property

steps.title: Proof from a גט thrown into her lap
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers that the buyer acquires, and proves it from the משנה about a גט thrown into a woman's lap or basket.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: you already learned it. If he threw it into her lap or into her basket, she is divorced.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers from a משנה about גיטין. A woman is divorced when her husband throws the גט into her lap or basket.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her lap or basket counts as hers even when she stands in her husband's space. The same logic says the buyer's vessel counts as his even on the seller's property, so the buyer acquires.

keyTerms.meaning: You have learned it (in a משנה)

phrases.english: He said to him: You learned it:
phrases.notes: This quotes a משנה in גיטין 77a about giving a גט.

phrases.english: If he threw it to her into her lap
or into her basket,
this woman is divorced.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's question from step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The buyer acquires, just as a woman's basket acquires the גט for her even in her husband's space.

steps.title: רב נחמן: that משנה is too weak to prove anything
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן objects that the משנה about the גט has been qualified so many times that it cannot be used as a proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: why did you answer him from that משנה, which has been hit with a hundred hammer blows?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן attacks רב הונא's proof. He says that משנה has been explained with so many conditions that it cannot settle this question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן is not giving the opposite ruling. He is rejecting the source. The hammer image means the משנה was reshaped by many limits, so its plain meaning cannot be relied on.
steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן is attacking the proof, not ruling that the buyer does not acquire. The גמרא goes on to try other sources for רב ששת's question in steps 10 and 16.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to him:
What is the reason you resolved it for him from that one,
which has been struck with a hundred hammer blows?
phrases.notes: It's a picture: the משנה has been explained with so many conditions that it no longer means what it seems to say.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן: מַאי טַעְמָא פָּשְׁטַתְּ לֵיהּ מֵהַהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof רב הונא brought in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's use of the משנה about the גט as a proof
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That משנה has been given so many qualifications that its plain meaning cannot support a ruling.

steps.title: The many conditions placed on the basket case
steps.stepSummary: Four אמוראים each limit the משנה of the גט in the basket to a special situation.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל says the basket must be hanging on her. ריש לקיש says it is enough if it is tied to her, even if it is not hanging. רב אדא בר אהבה says it was resting between her thighs. רב משרשיא says her husband sold baskets.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows why רב נחמן said the גט case was 'qualified so many times': here are the qualifications. Each one makes the basket case special, so it is not a plain example of a vessel sitting in someone else's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every opinion explains why the basket works without relying on the idea that 'your vessel acquires for you even in someone else's property.' Either the basket counts as part of her body (hanging, tied, between her thighs), or the husband doesn't mind where it sits (he sells baskets). That takes away רב הונא's proof.
steps.confusionAlert: These are not new arguments against each other in this sugya. The גמרא lists them together only to show how limited the basket case is.

phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
This applies only when her basket was hanging on her.
phrases.notes: "This" means the משנה in גיטין about a גט thrown into her basket.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said: tied to her,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינָהּ תְּלוּיָה בַּהּ.
phrases.english: even though it is not hanging from her.
Rav Adda bar Ahava said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיְתָה קַלְתָּהּ מוּנַּחַת לָהּ בֵּין יַרְכוֹתֶיהָ.
phrases.english: For example, where her basket was resting between her thighs.

phrases.aramaic: רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiya, son of Rabbi Ami, said:
For example, where her husband was a basket seller.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the evidence for רב נחמן's claim in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן's claim that the גט case is too qualified to prove anything.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The limiting statements of שמואל, ריש לקיש, רב אדא בר אהבה and רב משרשיא.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's view and רבא's reason
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the spot of her lap and her basket count as hers, and רבא explains that people do not mind about such small spots.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: the place of her lap belongs to her, and the place of her basket belongs to her. רבא said: what is his reason? Because a person does not mind about the place of her lap or the place of her basket.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more explanation of the basket case. This one says she has rights to that small spot, so the basket is not truly in someone else's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יוחנן, the basket works because the husband is treated as letting her have that spot. So this case also says nothing about a vessel in a property where its owner has no rights. This finishes knocking out רב הונא's proof.

keyTerms.meaning: the place of her lap, the spot where she sits or stands
belongs to her, is acquired for her

steps.whatToRemember: The basket case works only for special reasons (it is attached to her, or she has rights to the spot), so it cannot prove that a buyer's vessel acquires in the seller's property.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
The place of her lap belongs to her,
and the place of her basket belongs to her.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן?
phrases.english: Rava said: What is Rabbi Yochanan's reason?
Because a person does not mind
neither about the place of her lap
nor about the place of her basket.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: מְקוֹם חֵיקָהּ קָנוּי לָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds one more limiting explanation to the list in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That the גט case cannot prove רב הונא's point.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's statement and רבא's explanation of it.

steps.title: A new proof from a ברייתא about the seller's domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer רב ששת's question from a ברייתא that says that in the seller's domain the buyer acquires only by lifting the item or taking it out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Instead, answer the question from this: In the seller's domain, the buyer does not acquire until he lifts it or takes it out of the seller's domain. Isn't this talking about the buyer's vessels?
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גט proof fell apart, the גמרא tries a new source. It suggests that the ברייתא is talking about items in the buyer's own vessels, which would mean that his vessels do not acquire for him in the seller's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא is about the buyer's vessels, then it directly answers the question: no, the buyer does not acquire. This is the opposite of what רב הונא said.

keyTerms.meaning: answer the question from this source

phrases.english: Rather, resolve it from this:
In the seller's domain, he does not acquire
until he lifts it
or until he takes it out of the seller's domain.
What, is it not talking about the buyer's vessels?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the גט proof is rejected, a new source is brought for רב ששת's question.
steps.raayaObject: That a buyer's vessels in the seller's property do not acquire for him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: in the seller's domain, acquisition happens only by lifting or removing.

steps.title: The ברייתא may be about the seller's vessels
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: the ברייתא could be talking about items in the seller's own vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about the seller's vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof by giving a different picture of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the items sit in the seller's vessels in the seller's property, it is obvious that the buyer must lift them or take them out. So the ברייתא tells us nothing about the buyer's own vessels.

phrases.english: No, it is talking about the seller's vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the first clause of the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as talking about the seller's vessels, which would not answer the question.

steps.title: The second clause doesn't fit the seller's vessels
steps.stepSummary: If the first clause is about the seller's vessels, the second clause should be too. But then why does the buyer acquire in his own domain?
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the first clause is about the seller's vessels, the second clause should also be about the seller's vessels. But the second clause says: in the buyer's domain, once the seller agrees, the buyer acquires. If it is the seller's vessels, why does the buyer acquire?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rejection from step 11 by looking at the ברייתא's second clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption is that both clauses describe the same kind of vessel. But the seller's vessels should keep the item in the seller's hands, so the buyer should not acquire just because the item is in his domain. So reading both clauses as being about the seller's vessels seems wrong.

phrases.english: But since the first clause is about the seller's vessels,
the last clause should also be about the seller's vessels;
read the last clause: In the buyer's domain,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁקִּיבֵּל עָלָיו מוֹכֵר – קָנָה לוֹקֵחַ.
phrases.english: once the seller has agreed, the buyer acquires.
And if it is in the seller's vessels,
why does the buyer acquire?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִדְּרֵישָׁא בְּכִלְיוֹ דְמוֹכֵר סֵיפָא נָמֵי בְּכִלְיוֹ דְמוֹכֵר
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of the ברייתא as talking about the seller's vessels.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both clauses should share one setting. In the second clause, the seller's vessels would not let the buyer acquire, but the ברייתא says he does acquire.

steps.title: The second clause switches to the buyer's vessels
steps.stepSummary: The last clause is talking about a different case: the buyer's vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the last clause, we have come to the buyer's vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two clauses do not describe the same kind of vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause is about the seller's vessels, and the second is about the buyer's vessels. So the rejection in step 11 still stands, and the ברייתא still does not answer רב ששת's question.

keyTerms.meaning: we have come to (a new case)

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא can be read with its first clause about the seller's vessels and its last clause about the buyer's vessels, so it does not settle the question.

phrases.english: In the last clause, we have come to the buyer's vessels.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the clauses: each clause describes a different case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses must be about the same kind of vessel.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause is about the seller's vessels and the last clause is about the buyer's vessels.

steps.title: Why did the ברייתא not say which vessels it means?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 13. If the two clauses of the ברייתא are about different vessels, the ברייתא should have said so, but it speaks without qualification.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did the ברייתא state it without qualification?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer. If the first half is about the seller's vessels and the second half is about the buyer's vessels, why does the ברייתא not spell that out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13 the גמרא said the two clauses describe two different cases. The problem is that the wording of the ברייתא gives no hint of a change in vessels. A ברייתא normally tells us when the case changes, so the silence is a difficulty.

keyTerms.meaning: It stated it as a flat, unqualified rule
And why / and what is the reason

phrases.english: And why did it state it without qualification?
phrases.notes: Literally, 'why did it cut it off flat?' He means: why didn't the ברייתא say which vessels it is talking about?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 13, which split the ברייתא into two different vessel cases.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 13 that the last clause is about the buyer's vessels while the first is about the seller's vessels.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the cases differ, the ברייתא's unqualified wording is misleading; it should have said which vessels each clause means.

steps.title: The ברייתא describes the usual situation
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא did not need to name the vessels, because normally the seller's vessels are found in the seller's house and the buyer's vessels are found in the buyer's house.
steps.simpleTranslation: The normal way of things is that in the seller's house, the seller's vessels are usually found, and in the buyer's house, the buyer's vessels are usually found.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is simply describing what usually happens. In each person's house, his own vessels are the ones normally there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spoke about the ordinary case, so it did not need to mention vessels. 'Seller's domain' naturally means the seller's vessels, and 'buyer's domain' naturally means the buyer's vessels. This keeps the reading from step 11 and step 13, so the ברייתא cannot prove anything about רב ששת's question.

keyTerms.meaning: The usual, ordinary way things are

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about acquiring in the seller's domain versus the buyer's domain is really about whose vessels the goods are in. So it does not answer רב ששת's question, and רבא tries another proof in the next step.

phrases.english: The normal way of things is:
in the seller's house, the seller's vessels are commonly found;
in the buyer's house, the buyer's vessels are commonly found.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14 and closes the attempted proof from the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the text speaks about the ordinary case, so no qualification was needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the ברייתא did not mention vessels, both clauses should be about the same vessels, so splitting them (seller's vessels in the first clause, buyer's vessels in the last) seems forced.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא assumes the usual situation: each person's own vessels are in his own house. So its first clause is about the seller's vessels, and it says nothing about the buyer's vessels in the seller's domain.

steps.title: רבא brings a ברייתא about donkey drivers and laborers
steps.stepSummary: רבא tries a new proof for רב ששת's question. A ברייתא says that if a buyer pulled the donkey drivers and laborers carrying the goods into his house, whether he set the price before measuring or measured before setting the price, both sides can still back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Come and hear: If he pulled his donkey drivers and his laborers and brought them into his house, whether he set the price before he measured, or measured before he set the price, both of them can back out.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new attempt to answer רב ששת's question. He quotes a ברייתא where the goods are still on the donkeys and laborers, but they are already inside the buyer's house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the goods are inside the buyer's domain, but they are still being carried by the seller's donkeys and workers. The ברייתא rules that, as things stand, neither side is locked in. The גמרא is setting up a close reading of this ruling to see what it teaches about רב ששת's question.

keyTerms.meaning: To back out of the deal

phrases.english: Rava said: Come and hear:
If he pulled his donkey drivers and his laborers,
phrases.notes: The donkeys and the workers are carrying the goods he wants to buy, so pulling them brings the goods along.

phrases.english: and brought them into his house;
phrases.notes: 'His house' means the buyer's house, which is the buyer's domain.

phrases.english: whether he set the price before he measured,
or he measured before he set the price,
both of them can back out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof (steps 10–15) failed, רבא brings a different ברייתא to try to answer רב ששת's question.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's question whether a buyer's vessels acquire for him while they are in the seller's domain.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a buyer who pulled the seller's donkey drivers and laborers, still carrying the goods, into his own house, where both sides can still back out.
